title: Annexation, 1849
hookLine: after two wars with the British, Punjab is annexed and the boy king Duleep Singh sent to England

cards: A ten-year-old boy sits on a throne too big for him. He's the king, officially. His mother has been taken from him.
Grown men decide his future over his head. One spring day in 1849, he's asked to sign a paper that gives away his kingdom, and a diamond well-known across the world.
A few years later, he'll be living in England, thousands of miles from Punjab. Today: annexation, and the boy king Duleep Singh.

teach.b: After Ranjit Singh died in 1839, his kingdom fell into a decade of turmoil: rulers came and went, and several were killed. The British East India Company, already ruling much of India, was watching.
Two wars with the British followed, in 1845 and 1848. The Sikh armies fought hard, and some battles cost the British dearly. But the kingdom lost.
In March 1849, Punjab was annexed, taken into British India.
The last Maharaja, Duleep Singh, Ranjit Singh's youngest son, was about ten.

teach.h: A WEEK FROM LOSS TO GOLD TO EXILE.
teach.b: He was separated from his mother, Maharani Jind Kaur, and placed with a British guardian, and the Koh-i-Noor diamond was sent to Queen Victoria.
As a young teenager he became a Christian, and at fifteen he was taken to England, where he lived as a country gentleman.
As a young man he was allowed to bring his mother to England, and she lived near him until her death. Years later, in his forties, he tried to return to Punjab and took up his Sikh faith once more.
He was stopped on the way, and died in Paris in 1893, far from home. Sikhs remember him with a particular ache: the king who lost his home, his mother and his kingdom as a child. Now the week.
The Chhota Ghallughara: remembered. Gurmata: decide together. Baba Deep Singh: finish the vow.
The Vadda Ghallughara: the panth rose again. The misls: twelve, and one. Ranjit Singh: the golden temple.

how: Sikhs remember the annexation of 1849 as the end of the Sikh kingdom; Maharaja Duleep Singh's story is widely told in the Sikh diaspora, especially in Britain, where a statue of him stands in Thetford, Norfolk.

practice: Think of someone far from home right now: a friend who moved abroad, a grandparent who left their village long ago, a student in a new city, a soldier, a refugee you've read about.
Picture them where they are this evening, and what they might miss most, a food, a language, a face, a sound. Hold them there with kindness for a few breaths, and if you pray, hold them in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Annexation. In 1849, after two wars, Punjab was taken into British India, and the boy king Duleep Singh was later sent to England, far from home.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Punjab, from Persian panj (five) and aab (waters): the land of five rivers.

carryVoice: Your line: far from home. A week from loss, to gold, to exile. Day two hundred ninety-four, and a week complete.
